newsitem.title: USA: MCI-British Telcom set sights on Brazil, Mexico.
newsitem.headline: MCI-British Telcom set sights on Brazil, Mexico.

text.p: Brazil and Mexico head the list of Latin American markets targeted as top priorities in the alliance of Spanish telephone company Telefonica with British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp., executives said Friday.

"The deal will allow us to continue to expand into the two main markets in Latin America -- Brazil and Mexico," said Fernando Panizo, managing director of TISA, the overseas holding company of Spanish national phone company Telefonica.
Under the deal, Telefonica agreed to form a 50-50 Pan American joint venture with British Telecom and Washington-based MCI managed by TISA.

Britain's largest phone company and MCI, the second largest long distance phone company in the United States, announced in November that they had agreed to merge in a $20 billion deal to form a company called Concert.

The Pan-American deal represents the first part of a two-stage strategic alliance, Panizo said. The second stage will focus on Europe, where Telefonica and British Telecom are considering joint investments in various European countries, he said.
Telefonica must first extricate itself from its ties with with the AT&T Corp.-led Unisource consortium of European phone companies, which competes with the British Telecom-MCI Concert group.

Telefonica already holds significant stakes ranging in size from 22 percent to 44 percent in leading local, long-distance and wireless operators in Argentina, Chile, Columbia and Peru. TISA also owns a 13.5 percent stake in a regional Brazilian telecommunications company.
Now, as part of its pact with Concert, Telefonica plans to take a one-third stake in Avantel, MCI's long-distance venture with finacial services company Banamex in Mexico.
Panizo acknowledged several previous efforts by Telefonica to gain a foothold in Mexico had failed.

Telefonica, known for its expertise in building local phone services and marketing its products to Spanish-speaking markets, promises to transform Avantel into the leading full-service phone rival to state-owned Telmex.

Brazil is widely seen as the Latin American market with the largest potential for growth, with recent moves to open up long distance, wireless and data services markets and a raging debate over the breakup of local phone monopolies.
Panizo said the new joint venture will be coordinated to take advantage of alliances announced earlier this week that interconnect Portugal Telecom with both British Telecom-MCI and Telefonica.
In Brazil, this network of alliances, anticipates the breakup of Telebras SA, Brazil's national phone holding company, into four or five regional local phone providers.
"With the liberalisation of the market and the separation of Telebras ... we see an opportunity to bid for those companies we consider relevant to our strategy," Panizo said.
Lending weight to the strategy is Portugal Telecom's existing joint venture with the government-controlled Telebras.

Panizo sees the potential audience of the Pan-American joint venture's services numbering 500 million people, including 300 million Telefonica ventures already serve and the 30 million Spanish speakers living in the United States.
The Pan American pact builds on MCI's existing links between North and South America.
"There is a huge market for us in both directions," Tim Price, MCI's president, said in an interview.

"The deal gives us entry into a $36 billion Latin American market that is expected to grow to $60 billion in the next three years," Price said of market estimates for the year 2000. "This will give us a seamless network from the Cape to the North Pole," he boasted.
